items.stem: Which of the following best describes "common difference"?
options: The constant d = uₙ₊₁ − uₙ between consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence
The constant r = uₙ₊₁ ÷ uₙ of a geometric sequence
A sequence in which each term is obtained by multiplying the previous term by a constant common ratio r
An infinite series whose partial sums approach a finite limit
items.answer: The constant d = uₙ₊₁ − uₙ between consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence
items.markingKey: A. "common difference" is the constant d = uₙ₊₁ − uₙ between consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence.

items.stem: A graduate engineer in Melbourne earns 54000 AUD in the first year, with a fixed annual increase of 1900 AUD. Leila calculates the value for year 17 as 54000 + 17 × 1900 = 86300. Explain the mistake and find the correct value.
items.markingKey: R1 there are 16 differences between year 1 and year 17, not 17; M1 u17 = 54000 + 16 × 1900; A1 84400.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain the reasoning behind the formula Sₙ = n/2 (u₁ + uₙ).
items.answer: Write the series forwards and backwards and add: each of the n pairs sums to u₁ + uₙ, so 2Sₙ = n(u₁ + uₙ). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Write the series forwards and backwards and add: each of the n pairs sums to u₁ + uₙ, so 2Sₙ = n(u₁ + uₙ). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "In an arithmetic series, if uₙ is negative then Sₙ must also be negative." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Sₙ adds all terms; earlier positive terms can outweigh later negative terms, so Sₙ can still be positive.
items.markingKey: Sₙ adds all terms; earlier positive terms can outweigh later negative terms, so Sₙ can still be positive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "The 20th term of 5, 9, 13, … is 5 + 20 × 4 = 85." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: There are only 19 steps from u₁ to u₂₀: u₂₀ = 5 + 19 × 4 = 81.
items.markingKey: There are only 19 steps from u₁ to u₂₀: u₂₀ = 5 + 19 × 4 = 81. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "arithmetic sequence".
items.answer: A sequence in which each term is obtained from the previous one by adding a constant common difference d
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a sequence in which each term is obtained from the previous one by adding a constant common difference d. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which formula gives the nth term of an arithmetic sequence?
items.markingKey: A. There are n − 1 steps of size d from u₁ to uₙ.

items.stem: Explain why the graph of uₙ against n for an arithmetic sequence consists of points on a straight line.
items.answer: uₙ = u₁ + (n − 1)d = dn + (u₁ − d) is linear in n with gradient d, so the points (n, uₙ) are collinear (but discrete).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: uₙ = u₁ + (n − 1)d = dn + (u₁ − d) is linear in n with gradient d, so the points (n, uₙ) are collinear (but discrete). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why repeated percentage increases produce a geometric sequence rather than an arithmetic one.
items.answer: An increase of p% multiplies the current value by (1 + p/100); the same multiplier each step gives a constant ratio, so the amount added grows as the value grows.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: An increase of p% multiplies the current value by (1 + p/100); the same multiplier each step gives a constant ratio, so the amount added grows as the value grows. items.markingKey: A. S∞ exists only when |r| < 1.

items.stem: Diego uses S∞ = u₁/(1 − r) with u₁ = 48 and r = −2 to claim the series has sum 16.0. Explain why this is incorrect.

items.stem: Explain how the formula S∞ = u₁/(1 − r) follows from Sₙ = u₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r).
items.answer: When |r| < 1, rⁿ → 0 as n → ∞, so Sₙ → u₁(1 − 0)/(1 − r).

items.stem: "Because the series 1 + 0.9 + 0.81 + … has infinitely many terms, its sum must be infinite." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Infinitely many terms can have a finite sum when they shrink fast enough: r = 0.9 gives S∞ = 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10.
items.markingKey: Infinitely many terms can have a finite sum when they shrink fast enough: r = 0.9 gives S∞ = 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the reasoning behind the formula Sₙ = n/2 (u₁ + uₙ).
items.answer: Write the series forwards and backwards and add: each of the n pairs sums to u₁ + uₙ, so 2Sₙ = n(u₁ + uₙ).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Write the series forwards and backwards and add: each of the n pairs sums to u₁ + uₙ, so 2Sₙ = n(u₁ + uₙ). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why a geometric sequence with 0 < r < 1 has terms that decrease but never become negative.
items.answer: Each term is a positive fraction of the one before; multiplying a positive number by a positive r < 1 makes it smaller but still positive, so the terms approach 0.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each term is a positive fraction of the one before; multiplying a positive number by a positive r < 1 makes it smaller but still positive, so the terms approach 0. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Because the series 1 + 0.9 + 0.81 + … has infinitely many terms, its sum must be infinite." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Infinitely many terms can have a finite sum when they shrink fast enough: r = 0.9 gives S∞ = 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10.
items.markingKey: Infinitely many terms can have a finite sum when they shrink fast enough: r = 0.9 gives S∞ = 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Ingrid invests 5000 NZD at 3.1% per annum. Show that the yearly values form an arithmetic sequence under simple interest and a geometric sequence under annual compound interest, stating d and r in each case.
items.markingKey: Simple: value increases by 5000 × 3.1/100 = 155.00 each year (constant difference) (R1 A1). Compound: value multiplied by 1.031 each year (constant ratio) (R1 A1).

items.stem: Lukas writes: "In an arithmetic series, if uₙ is negative then Sₙ must also be negative." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Sₙ adds all terms; earlier positive terms can outweigh later negative terms, so Sₙ can still be positive.
items.markingKey: Sₙ adds all terms; earlier positive terms can outweigh later negative terms, so Sₙ can still be positive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "A value that increases by 5% per year for 10 years increases by 50% in total." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Growth compounds: 1.05¹⁰ = 1.63, an increase of about 63%, not 50%.
items.markingKey: Growth compounds: 1.05¹⁰ = 1.63, an increase of about 63%, not 50%. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "The series 4 − 2 + 1 − 0.5 + … has no sum to infinity because the terms change sign." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.markingKey: r = −0.5 and |r| < 1, so S∞ = 4/(1 + 0.5) = 8/3. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: There are only 19 steps from u₁ to u₂₀: u₂₀ = 5 + 19 × 4 = 81.
items.markingKey: There are only 19 steps from u₁ to u₂₀: u₂₀ = 5 + 19 × 4 = 81. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: (a) A = 16900(1 + 3.4n/100), B = 16900(1.028)ⁿ (b) 15 years (c) A is better over 11 years

items.stem: Which formula gives the nth term of a geometric sequence?
items.markingKey: B. There are n − 1 multiplications by r from u₁ to uₙ.

items.stem: What happens to rⁿ as n → ∞ when |r| < 1?
items.markingKey: It tends to 0. Repeated multiplication by a number of size less than 1 makes the result shrink towards 0.

items.stem: Explain why an arithmetic model of a person's savings may be unrealistic over a long period.
items.answer: It assumes the same increase every period forever; in reality income, spending and interest change, and savings usually grow by percentages (geometric) rather than fixed amounts.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It assumes the same increase every period forever; in reality income, spending and interest change, and savings usually grow by percentages (geometric) rather than fixed amounts. items.stem: Logs are stacked in layers; the bottom layer has 25 logs and each layer above has 1 fewer. Explain why the numbers of logs in successive layers form an arithmetic sequence, and interpret the values of u₁ and d in this context.
items.answer: Constant change of -1 logs per layer; u₁ = 25 logs in the first layer, d = -1.
